title: Male reproductive system
blurb: Trace sperm from the seminiferous tubules to the urethra, match each gland and cell to its job, and explain how FSH, LH and testosterone control the testes.
question: After a vasectomy, a patient still ejaculates a normal-looking volume of semen, yet a lab test finds no sperm in it. Which structure was cut, and why is semen still produced?

teach.body: The male reproductive system makes sperm and testosterone in the testes, matures and stores sperm, moves them through a series of ducts, and mixes them with fluid from accessory glands to form semen. Sperm are gametes: made by meiosis, they are haploid (n = 23). Fertilization restores the diploid number (2n = 46). The sperm decides the baby's sex, because it carries either an X or a Y; the egg always carries an X.

teach.h: Inside the testis: two key cell types
teach.caption: Seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis. Sertoli cells also release inhibin, which inhibits FSH.

teach.h: Why the testes hang outside the body
teach.body: The testes sit in the scrotum, outside the abdominopelvic cavity, which keeps them about 2-3 °C below core body temperature. Sperm production needs that slightly cooler environment. So the location is a temperature-control feature, not a design accident.

steps.label: Ductus (vas) deferens
steps.sub: Through inguinal canal; cut in vasectomy

teach.caption: The urethra carries both urine and semen, but not at the same time.
Epididymis comes BEFORE vas deferens, and the ejaculatory duct comes BEFORE the urethra.

head: Gland
Secretion
Key fact
rows: About 60% of semen; fructose fuels sperm
Milky, slightly acidic fluid with enzymes (PSA)
Surrounds the urethra below the bladder

teach.caption: Most semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles, not the prostate.

teach.h: A sperm cell has three parts
teach.body: The head holds the nucleus with 23 chromosomes, capped by the acrosome, which contains enzymes that let the sperm penetrate the egg. The midpiece is packed with mitochondria that make ATP for movement. The tail is a flagellum that drives the sperm forward. Plain English: the head carries the DNA and the key, the midpiece is the engine, and the tail is the propeller.

teach.caption: Testosterone drives sperm production, male secondary sex characteristics and libido. It feeds back negatively on the hypothalamus and pituitary; inhibin from Sertoli cells inhibits FSH.

teach.body: Mr. Robinson has a vasectomy: each ductus (vas) deferens is cut. His testes still make sperm and testosterone, but sperm can no longer travel past the cut. The seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands all add their fluid farther along the route, so he still ejaculates semen. It simply contains no sperm. His testosterone, made by Leydig cells and carried in the blood, is unaffected.

teach.text: Sperm are MADE in the seminiferous tubules and only MATURED and STORED in the epididymis. Leydig cells make testosterone; Sertoli cells nurse sperm. LH targets Leydig cells; FSH targets Sertoli cells. The seminal vesicles, not the prostate, supply most of the semen.

items: Gametes are haploid (23); fertilization restores 46; the sperm's X or Y sets the sex.
Seminiferous tubules make sperm (Sertoli cells nurse them); Leydig cells make testosterone.
Route: tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra.
Seminal vesicles (about 60%, fructose), prostate (PSA), bulbourethral (pre-ejaculate mucus).
GnRH, then FSH (Sertoli) and LH (Leydig); testosterone and inhibin feed back negatively.

summary: You can now trace sperm from the seminiferous tubules through the epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra, and name what each accessory gland adds. You can also match Sertoli and Leydig cells to FSH and LH and explain the parts of a sperm cell.

A.why: Spermatogenesis takes place in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, supported by Sertoli cells.

whyNot.0: The epididymis matures and stores sperm; it does not produce them.
whyNot.2: The vas deferens transports sperm from the epididymis toward the ejaculatory duct.
whyNot.3: The seminal vesicles secrete most of the fluid in semen, not sperm.

A.q: Which cells in the testes secrete testosterone?
A.why: Interstitial (Leydig) cells, between the seminiferous tubules, make testosterone when stimulated by LH.

whyNot.1: Sertoli cells nurse developing sperm and release inhibin; they do not make testosterone.
whyNot.2: The epididymis matures and stores sperm; it is not a testosterone source.
whyNot.3: The prostate secretes a milky fluid with enzymes such as PSA, not testosterone.

A.q: Which structure supplies about 60% of semen volume as a fructose-rich alkaline fluid?
A.why: The seminal vesicles provide most of the semen: an alkaline fluid rich in fructose (sperm fuel) plus prostaglandins.

whyNot.0: The prostate adds a milky, slightly acidic fluid with enzymes, but less of the volume.
whyNot.1: The bulbourethral glands secrete a small amount of clear mucus before ejaculation.
whyNot.3: The epididymis stores and matures sperm; it is not the main fluid source.

B.q: Which sequence shows the path of sperm from production to exit?
options: Seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, urethra
Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, ejaculatory duct
Epididymis, seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra
Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra
B.why: Sperm are made in the tubules, mature in the epididymis, travel the vas deferens, enter the ejaculatory duct, then leave via the urethra.

whyNot.0: The epididymis comes before the vas deferens, not after it.
whyNot.1: The ejaculatory duct empties into the urethra, so it must come first.
whyNot.2: Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules before reaching the epididymis.

B.q: Which part of a sperm cell contains enzymes that help it penetrate the egg?
B.why: The acrosome caps the head and holds the enzymes used to penetrate the egg.

whyNot.0: The midpiece holds mitochondria that make ATP for movement.
whyNot.1: The nucleus carries the 23 chromosomes, not the penetrating enzymes.

B.q: Which statement about hormonal control of the testes is CORRECT?
options: LH stimulates Leydig cells to make testosterone
FSH stimulates Leydig cells to make testosterone
LH stimulates Sertoli cells to release inhibin
GnRH is released by the anterior pituitary
B.why: LH from the anterior pituitary acts on the interstitial (Leydig) cells, which secrete testosterone.

whyNot.1: FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis, not on Leydig cells.
whyNot.2: LH targets Leydig cells; Sertoli cells respond to FSH and release inhibin, which inhibits FSH.
whyNot.3: GnRH comes from the hypothalamus; the anterior pituitary releases FSH and LH.

C.q: After a vasectomy, Mr. Robinson still ejaculates semen, but it contains no sperm. Which statement BEST explains this?
options: The epididymis is removed, so sperm are not stored
The vas deferens is cut, but the glands still secrete
The prostatic urethra is tied, so sperm cannot exit
The seminiferous tubules are tied, so sperm production ends
C.why: Cutting the vas deferens blocks sperm, while the seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands, which join farther along, still add their fluid.

whyNot.0: A vasectomy cuts the vas deferens; the epididymis is left in place.
whyNot.2: Tying the urethra would block urine and all semen, not just sperm.
whyNot.3: The testes keep producing sperm after a vasectomy; sperm simply cannot pass the cut.

C.q: Which statement about the male accessory glands is CORRECT?
options: The prostate produces most of the volume of semen
Bulbourethral glands secrete mucus before ejaculation
Seminal vesicles secrete an acidic, fructose-free fluid
The prostate lies above the bladder, around the ureters
C.why: The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands release clear mucus before ejaculation, which neutralizes acidic urine residue in the urethra.

whyNot.0: The seminal vesicles, not the prostate, produce most of the semen (about 60%).
whyNot.2: Seminal vesicle fluid is alkaline and rich in fructose.
whyNot.3: The prostate lies below the bladder and surrounds the urethra.

C.q: A sperm cell and an egg cell each carry 23 chromosomes. Which statement BEST explains this?
options: Gametes are haploid, so fertilization restores 46
Gametes are diploid, so fertilization doubles to 92
Gametes form by mitosis, so they keep half the set
Gametes are haploid, so the zygote also has 23
C.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so gametes are haploid (n = 23); fertilization combines two sets to restore the diploid 46.

whyNot.1: Gametes are haploid, not diploid; 46 is the diploid number of body cells.
whyNot.2: Gametes form by meiosis; mitosis keeps the full chromosome number.
whyNot.3: The zygote receives 23 from each parent, giving 46, not 23.

reteach.title: Think of a factory and its shipping route
reteach.question: Picture a factory that builds products, finishes them in a warehouse, trucks them down a highway and packs them in shipping fluid. Which male structure plays each role?

blocks.body: The seminiferous tubules are the factory floor where products (sperm) are built, with Sertoli cells as the floor supervisors. Leydig cells are the office next door sending out the company memo: testosterone. The epididymis is the finishing warehouse where products mature and wait. The vas deferens is the highway, the ejaculatory duct is the merge lane where the seminal vesicle trucks add fuel, and the urethra is the final exit road.

blocks.text: The warehouse does not build anything: the epididymis stores and matures sperm, it does not make them.

explain.body: Seminiferous tubules make sperm, supported by Sertoli cells; Leydig cells between the tubules make testosterone. The scrotum keeps the testes about 2-3 °C cooler than the body core.

test.q: Why are the testes held in the scrotum, outside the abdominopelvic cavity?
options: Testosterone breaks down at normal body temperature
The scrotum supplies the fructose that sperm need
Cooler tissue lets testosterone enter the blood faster
Sperm production needs a slightly lower temperature
test.why: Spermatogenesis needs a temperature about 2-3 °C below core body temperature, which the scrotum provides.

whyNot.0: Testosterone circulates throughout the warm body; the scrotum's role is about sperm production.
whyNot.1: Fructose comes from the seminal vesicles, not the scrotum.
whyNot.2: The scrotum's cooler temperature serves sperm production, not hormone release into the blood.

explain.body: Seminiferous tubules, epididymis (matures and stores), vas deferens (cut in vasectomy), ejaculatory duct, urethra.

test.q: Sperm complete their maturation and are stored in the
test.why: The epididymis is where sperm mature and are stored until ejaculation.

whyNot.0: The seminiferous tubules produce sperm; maturation happens afterward in the epididymis.
whyNot.2: The ejaculatory duct is a short passage where sperm meet seminal vesicle fluid; it is not a storage site.
whyNot.3: The seminal vesicles secrete fluid; they do not store sperm.

explain.body: Seminal vesicles: about 60% of semen, fructose, alkaline. Prostate: milky, slightly acidic, PSA. Bulbourethral: clear mucus before ejaculation.

test.q: Which gland secretes a milky, slightly acidic fluid containing enzymes such as PSA?
test.why: The prostate secretes a milky, slightly acidic fluid with enzymes such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA).

whyNot.0: The seminal vesicles secrete an alkaline, fructose-rich fluid.
whyNot.1: The bulbourethral glands secrete clear mucus.
whyNot.3: The epididymis stores and matures sperm rather than secreting semen fluid.

explain.body: Hypothalamus releases GnRH. Anterior pituitary releases FSH (acts on Sertoli cells) and LH (acts on Leydig cells). Testosterone and inhibin feed back negatively.

test.q: Which hormone directly stimulates the interstitial (Leydig) cells to secrete testosterone?
test.why: Luteinizing hormone (LH) from the anterior pituitary targets Leydig cells.

whyNot.0: FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis.
whyNot.1: GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary, not directly on the testes.
whyNot.2: Inhibin comes from Sertoli cells and inhibits FSH release.
